creator: Chris Huber Reitz
name: Arizona Supreme Court — ACJA § 1-509 Use of Generative AI Technology and LLMs (AO 2024-207, amended AO 2025-24)
quote: Court personnel must review their AI-generated material for accuracy, completeness, and potentially erroneous, incomplete, hallucinated, biased, or otherwise problematic output. Court personnel must use caution when relying on the output.
quote_label: ACJA § 1-509(F)(4) Review of AI-Generated Material, adopted by Administrative Order No. 2024-207 (30 Oct 2024); applies to all court personnel

provenance.note: DISCONFIRMATION PROBE (synthetic identity inside a court). The Arizona judiciary publicly uses AI-generated avatar presenters for news releases; the code is silent on synthetic identity and on labeling AI presenters, so D4 stays at 1 (public-facing tools must be tested so 'false, illegal, or misleading information is not provided to the public'; hallucination named in F.4) and D3 at 1 (approval from the judicial officer before AI material is used in their work, I.1; no public labeling duty). The probe holds on paper: tolerance of synthetic presenters is consistent with a code that never names them. The permit/reserve line is drawn by confidentiality (sequestered vs non-sequestered systems, G) and by approved-tool lists (I), not by verification cost, hence c2 partially. D1=1: court-developed tools 'must document the source of the training information and generally how it works' (J); no provenance on outputs. D5=2: mandatory review (F.4), pre-deployment testing (H), judicial-officer approval (I.1). Purpose clause: 'To promote the use of Generative AI tools when it is beneficial and appropriate'. Twilight true: § L requires regular review 'to account for changes in AI technologies'. Governs court personnel, not litigants (mirror of the Singapore circular).
